title: Lex Cornelia de Sicariis et Veneficis — Sulla's Magic Law
description: Sulla's Lex Cornelia de sicariis et veneficis (81 BCE) constituted the foundational Roman criminal statute on poisoners and sorcerers, subsuming earlier provisions into a comprehensive legal framework. The law made veneficium (magic/poisoning) a capital crime prosecutable before permanent quaestiones (standing courts), establishing standardized procedures for such prosecutions. This legislation became the primary Roman legal authority on magic-related crimes and was transmitted through later compilations including the Digest of Justinian, profoundly shaping medieval and early modern European legal thinking about witchcraft. Its association of magic with assassination (sicarii) reinforced the image of the sorcerer as a social threat.
historiographical_note: Richard Gordon and Jan Bremmer have analyzed the Lex Cornelia as the critical Roman legal text transmitted to medieval jurists, noting how its conflation of poison and magic shaped the concept of the malevolent witch as legal category.
source_method: Published scholarship; Digest of Justinian 48.8; secondary legal history
